The real driver is an egress report showing 6,400 staff already pasting company data into consumer AI tools. The result owed is moving that use onto a governed platform, and the chatbot is only the feature. The hard constraint is two bars that pull against each other. The design buys the model and builds orchestration, connectors and governance around it. It centres on the context assembler, where permissions, cost, safety and quality meet: each turn is re-authorised, retrieval is filtered against the asker's live permissions, streamed output is scanned for secrets, and every turn writes an audit record.

sections.html:
1. Customer Problem and Discovery

The room
  • CIO: "Last month 6,400 employees reached consumer AI domains. We need one of our own."
  • General Counsel: wants proof that deal documents never reach a third party's training set, and a way to produce one person's history when legal process requires it.
  • Internal Comms: the previous chatbot drew 400 users who came once each. If ours is worse than free, people stay with free.
  • Platform lead: what do 40,000 seats cost each month, and who pays?
  • AI lead: plain chat is the easy bit. The hard part is grounding in internal systems within each person's permissions.
Feature vs. business result
  • The feature: a clone of ChatGPT.
  • The business result: close a data-leak risk nobody can see, and deliver a real productivity gain. Both must hold.
  • Weak way to start: "React frontend, vector DB, LLM (large language model) gateway." It lists parts and never says what they are for.
Stakeholders and what each judges
Stakeholder Judges on Fails if ignored
Employees Whether it helps within 90 seconds A governed tool that sits unused
Security / legal / compliance Evidence on egress, retention and discoverability The pilot stalls before production
Department admins / power users Whether they can build and share assistants The platform team turns into a ticket queue
Platform operators A single fleet they can operate that outlives any one vendor Cannot be run at 40k
Finance A cost per employee per month they can defend An unplanned budget review by month four
  • Jobs-to-be-done: summarise, draft, explain and find. The model already handles the first three; finding is where our engineering goes.
Six discovery questions that change the architecture
  1. Model sourcing: a commercial API, our own hosted model, or a mix split by data classification?
  2. Grounding scope: day one as plain chat, or with company systems too? If systems, which three lead?
  3. Retention and discovery: how long do we keep conversations, and who may read someone else's, through what process?
  4. Assistant publishing: may any employee publish an assistant, or does publishing need approval?
  5. Identity and residency: is SSO (single sign-on) the only login? Do we need regional deployments? Does a works council limit usage telemetry?
  6. Build vs. buy: what exactly stops us licensing a vendor's enterprise tier?

Interview pointer: Many candidates skip question 6, build vs. buy. Raise it yourself, before the interviewer does. In this scenario it is one of the strongest discovery signals you can give.

Assumption ledger (state aloud, don't bury)
  • Internal-confidential data may go to a commercial API that has a zero-retention agreement. Restricted data may not.
  • Identity comes only from corporate SSO.
  • We ground in three systems first: the intranet, the HR policy library and the engineering wiki.
  • Each conversation belongs to its employee, yet stays discoverable under legal hold.
Testable outcome
  • The target I would put forward: cut measured consumer-AI egress by 80% within two quarters, while weekly active use reaches 50%.
  • Why it holds up: neither a lockdown nor an ungoverned launch can meet it. Only a design that does both passes.
  • A rare advantage: the baseline already sits in the proxy logs. Most AI projects never settle whether they worked.
Two-minute opening (say this)

"The goal is to move AI usage off consumer tools and onto a governed platform, without losing what drew people there. I hold two bars. Nothing leaves our boundary unless an agreement we control covers it. And the time to first token roughly matches the free tools. First I'd clarify where the model comes from, the first systems to ground in, how long we keep conversations and who can read them, whether staff can publish assistants, and why we can't just buy. My default is a thin orchestration layer we own over a commercial API, with permission-filtered retrieval and a provider abstraction. Success means shadow-AI traffic falls and weekly active use climbs. A launch date is not success."

sections.title: 2. Requirements and Constraints
sections.text: 2. Requirements and ConstraintsThe trap Believing the scope. The product we are told to copy took years to build. It spans chat, memory, retrieval, voice, images, code execution and a marketplace. Lean hard on the exclusions bucket. Naming early what we will not build reads as strength. Sort everything into four buckets: functional, nonfunctional, explicit exclusions and hard constraints. Deep-dive questions → what each decides Question What it decides Model sourcing and data-processing terms Weeks of thin orchestration, or quarters spent also running a GPU fleet. Also whether the hot path needs a classification gate Grounding scope + are ACLs query-time resolvable? A single index versus federated connectors; pre-filter, post-filter or both. A source whose ACLs we cannot resolve waits for phase two, however keen its sponsor Retention, legal hold, eDiscovery The conversation store, a deletion pipeline, the audit schema, and an admin surface that is audited too Assistant publishing A chat app or a platform. A platform brings the harder authorisation problem: scope must stay within the viewer's permissions, not the creator's Identity, regions, workforce rules The deployment topology. In some jurisdictions, such as Germany and the Netherlands, the works council must approve per-employee telemetry before engineering even starts Build vs. buy Sometimes the honest answer is "buy", and the FDE who says so serves the customer well Functional requirements (must / should / could) Must: authenticated streaming chat with titles, history, branching and regeneration. Must: permission-aware retrieval that returns only documents the employee could already open, each with a citation. Must: model routing through a provider abstraction, so an outage or a deprecated model never forces a rewrite. Must: policy checks on input and output, covering both directions of each model call. Must: retention, legal hold and admin discovery, and each admin read goes into the audit log. Must: usage metering and per-user quotas. Every cost gets an owner, and a runaway script hits a ceiling. Should: custom assistants with their own instructions, tools and data. Governed when published, re-authorised whenever viewed. Could: an assistant marketplace, memory across conversations, images and voice. Safety goals as measurable behaviour No retrieval above the caller's access level. Nothing from a document they cannot open may surface: not a chunk, title, snippet, citation or cached answer, shared conversations included. No uncontrolled egress. Every permitted destination is listed, and the system enforces the list rather than trusting habit. A complete audit that reveals tampering. It must answer "who saw what, and when". Capped spend per user. A hard ceiling stops any account before it burns an unlimited budget. Explicit MVP exclusions Nothing writes to systems of record. The MVP (minimum viable product) reads and drafts. Agentic writes need a risk review of their own. We do not fine-tune on company data. We ground through retrieval, not weights. No line calms Legal more. No voice, no images, no code execution sandbox. Each is a product in its own right. No outside or customer access. Only employees signed in through SSO. No long-term memory across conversations. It needs a privacy consultation first. Question tree (walk this aloud in 2 minutes) Can prompts leave our boundary? No: self-host, plan GPUs, accept a lower quality bar and a longer timeline. Yes: thin orchestration, delivered in weeks. It depends: a classifier in the hot path and two backends. Do we ground on day one? No: launch plain chat within six weeks and measure demand. Yes: name the three sources and check their ACLs resolve at query time. Who may publish assistants? Nobody: a simpler build. Anyone: publish review, re-authorisation at view time and a deprecation lifecycle. What is wrong with buying? Nothing specific: recommend buying. A concrete constraint: it becomes the centre of the design. sections.title: 3. Scale, SLOs, and Capacity
sections.text: 3. Scale, SLOs, and CapacityLoad shape Expect enterprise chat traffic to be lumpy: a sharp spike from 8:30 to 10:00, a lunch dip, a smaller afternoon peak, and near silence overnight. My working numbers: 40,000 employees, of whom 12,000 are DAU (daily active users); each has 8 conversations a day, with 6 turns in each. That makes 576,000 turns a day, or 16 a second across a 10-hour day. With an assumed morning peak 2.5× higher, we reach about 40 turns a second. Plan for four things: average, peak, growth and skew. Build in growth headroom, because adoption is the goal. Skew comes from power users and scripts. The number that actually sizes the system A REST call at 40 requests a second, 50 ms each, keeps about 2 requests open. A chat stream at 40 turns a second, lasting an assumed 20 seconds, keeps 800 connections open. Application Load Balancer: AWS’s HTTP load balancer, which spreads requests across healthy service instances.

sections.title: 5. Data Model, APIs, and Code
sections.text: 5. Data Model, APIs, and CodeFive records Conversation(id, workspace_id, owner_id, assistant_id, title, retention_class, legal_hold, …): retention_class names a policy instead of holding a number, so legal can change the rule with no migration. Every deletion path must check legal_hold. Message(id, conversation_id, parent_id, role, content_ref, citations, token_count, model_id, status, …): messages form a tree rather than a list. parent_id lets a user regenerate a reply or edit and resend a turn. Pick a flat array and you will pay heavily to change it later. Assistant(id, author_id, instructions, tool_bindings, data_scopes, visibility, version, review_state): data_scopes is an upper bound. Published versions never change, so a conversation can record which version replied. Attachment(id, uploader_id, mime, size, scan_status, extract_ref, storage_ref, …): scan_status decides whether the file may enter the context window. A failed scan means unusable, never "probably fine". AuditEvent(event_id, actor_id, action, resource_ref, decision, reason, occurred_at): append-only, and admin reads are logged too. Framing: Conversation means ownership. Assistant means delegated authority. Attachment means untrusted input. AuditEvent means we can defend ourselves. Message is the work people will hate to lose. Why status matters: a stream that dies at 80% is not complete, blocked or failed; it is partial. Four endpoints POST /v1/conversations: starts a conversation. POST /v1/conversations/{id}/messages: adds a turn and streams the reply over SSE (server-sent events). This is the endpoint to get right. POST /v1/assistants/{id}/publish: a controlled state change, with optimistic concurrency keyed on version. GET /v1/admin/discovery: refuses calls without a case reference, and each search it runs is itself audited. On the streaming endpoint: Idempotency is mandatory: key it on (conversation_id, client_message_id). Send it twice and you get back the turn already stored, partial or not. Every event has a type: token, citation, route_change, blocked, done, error. Plain untyped text is out, because the client must tell a fallback notice apart from answer content. Errors: 403 when the caller lacks authorisation; 409 when a request with the same key is still running (422 when that key arrives with a different body); 413 for an oversized attachment; 429 for quota; a policy block that carries a reason code; 503 when every provider is down. A stream that opens with 200 and stops at token 300 has failed. Our SLI (service level indicator) looks for done events and ignores HTTP status codes. The riskiest component: the turn handler One skipped check here exposes a colleague's conversation, sends a document or secret to a vendor, or puts a card number on screen. It runs in eight steps: authorise → scan input → admit → assemble → route → stream with output scan → finalise idempotently → audit. SCAN_WINDOW, SCAN_OVERLAP = 256, 64 # overlap stops a pattern hiding on a boundary async def handle_turn(principal, req, conversations, policy, quota, assembler, router, audit): """Stream one turn. Yields typed SSE events, never raw text.""" # 1. Authorize THIS conversation on THIS turn — sharing and revocation # happen between turns, so a session-time check is not enough. await conversations.authorize(principal, req.conversation_id) # 2. Idempotency before any spend; a retry must not re-charge tokens. existing = await conversations.find_turn(req.conversation_id, req.client_message_id) if existing is not None: yield {"type": "done", "status": existing["status"], "replayed": True} return # 3. Input policy before any egress; a blocked turn creates no state. verdict = await policy.scan_input(principal, req.text, req.attachment_ids) if not verdict.allowed: await audit.emit(principal, "turn.blocked", req.conversation_id, "deny", verdict.reason) yield {"type": "blocked", "reason": verdict.reason} return turn_id = await conversations.begin_turn(principal, req) # 4. Assemble with the PRINCIPAL — retrieval permissions derive from the # asking human, never the assistant's author or a service account. ctx = await assembler.build(principal, req.conversation_id, req.text, verdict.classification) # 5. Admit on real input size — the raw message under-counts retrieval-heavy turns. await quota.admit(principal, ctx.input_tokens) # 6. Route on classification first, cost second. A cheaper provider that is # not approved for restricted data is not cheaper; it is an incident. route = await router.choose(classification=verdict.classification, input_tokens=ctx.input_tokens) yield {"type": "route", "model": route["model"]} for citation in ctx.citations: # provenance before tokens yield {"type": "citation", **citation} # 7. Stream with a sliding scan. One token cannot be judged; buffering the # whole answer would destroy the TTFT the product lives on. emitted, window, status = [], "", "complete" try: async for chunk in router.stream(route, ctx): window += chunk if len(window) >= SCAN_WINDOW: if not policy.scan_output_window(window).allowed: raise TurnBlocked("output_policy") window = window[-SCAN_OVERLAP:] emitted.append(chunk) yield {"type": "token", "text": chunk} if not policy.scan_output_window(window).allowed: raise TurnBlocked("output_policy") except TurnBlocked as blocked: status = "blocked" yield {"type": "blocked", "reason": blocked.reason, "partial": True} except Exception: # provider died mid-stream status = "failed" yield {"type": "error", "retryable": True} finally: # 8. Finalize on EVERY path — complete, blocked or failed. A turn that # vanishes without a record is both a billing hole and an audit hole. usage = {"input": ctx.input_tokens, "output": len(emitted)} await conversations.finalize_turn(turn_id, status=status, text="".join(emitted), citations=ctx.citations, usage=usage, route=route) await quota.record(principal, usage) await audit.emit(principal, "turn.completed", turn_id, status) yield {"type": "done", "status": status} This is a condensed sketch; a production build adds typed protocols and fuller comments. The lines that carry the design authorize(...) runs first, on every turn. A common slip is to check access when the session opens and then stop checking. assembler.build(principal, …): if you remember one line, make it this one. What the turn may see is derived from the person asking. quota.admit(…, ctx.input_tokens) comes after assembly, because the turns that pull in the most retrieved text are the expensive ones. router.choose(classification=…): data classification wins over price when picking a model. SCAN_OVERLAP: without it, a secret split across two scan windows gets through. Teams ship this bug all the time. finally: every path finalises the turn, records usage and writes audit. Code without this block would not survive in production. Idempotency, versioning, concurrency: three places, three reasons Turns: clients retry, and every token costs money. Assistant publishes: if two admins edit at once, neither may quietly clobber the other's change. Retention policy: years later, legal will want to know which policy was in force when a record was created. Failures the whiteboard sketch omits Client drops off mid-stream → cancel the provider's stream too, or you pay for tokens nobody reads. This happens often and wastes real money. Attachment still being scanned → wait, or go ahead and say so. If we carry on quietly, users assume the model ignored their file. Assembled context exceeds the budget → trim history, but never the head. Cutting from the front drops the system prompt in long conversations, and the governed assistant quietly turns into a bare model. Audit write fails → the turn fails too. 5. Data Model, APIs, and Code

Five records
  • Conversation(id, workspace_id, owner_id, assistant_id, title, retention_class, legal_hold, …): retention_class names a policy instead of holding a number, so legal can change the rule with no migration. Every deletion path must check legal_hold.
  • Message(id, conversation_id, parent_id, role, content_ref, citations, token_count, model_id, status, …): messages form a tree rather than a list. parent_id lets a user regenerate a reply or edit and resend a turn. Pick a flat array and you will pay heavily to change it later.
  • Assistant(id, author_id, instructions, tool_bindings, data_scopes, visibility, version, review_state): data_scopes is an upper bound. Published versions never change, so a conversation can record which version replied.
  • Attachment(id, uploader_id, mime, size, scan_status, extract_ref, storage_ref, …): scan_status decides whether the file may enter the context window. A failed scan means unusable, never "probably fine".
  • AuditEvent(event_id, actor_id, action, resource_ref, decision, reason, occurred_at): append-only, and admin reads are logged too.
  • Framing: Conversation means ownership. Assistant means delegated authority. Attachment means untrusted input. AuditEvent means we can defend ourselves. Message is the work people will hate to lose.
  • Why status matters: a stream that dies at 80% is not complete, blocked or failed; it is partial.
Four endpoints
  • POST /v1/conversations: starts a conversation.
  • POST /v1/conversations/{id}/messages: adds a turn and streams the reply over SSE (server-sent events). This is the endpoint to get right.
  • POST /v1/assistants/{id}/publish: a controlled state change, with optimistic concurrency keyed on version.
  • GET /v1/admin/discovery: refuses calls without a case reference, and each search it runs is itself audited.

On the streaming endpoint:

  • Idempotency is mandatory: key it on (conversation_id, client_message_id). Send it twice and you get back the turn already stored, partial or not.
  • Every event has a type: token, citation, route_change, blocked, done, error. Plain untyped text is out, because the client must tell a fallback notice apart from answer content.
  • Errors: 403 when the caller lacks authorisation; 409 when a request with the same key is still running (422 when that key arrives with a different body); 413 for an oversized attachment; 429 for quota; a policy block that carries a reason code; 503 when every provider is down.
  • A stream that opens with 200 and stops at token 300 has failed. Our SLI (service level indicator) looks for done events and ignores HTTP status codes.
The riskiest component: the turn handler
  • One skipped check here exposes a colleague's conversation, sends a document or secret to a vendor, or puts a card number on screen.
  • It runs in eight steps: authorise → scan input → admit → assemble → route → stream with output scan → finalise idempotently → audit.
SCAN_WINDOW, SCAN_OVERLAP = 256, 64   # overlap stops a pattern hiding on a boundary

async def handle_turn(principal, req, conversations, policy, quota,
                      assembler, router, audit):
    """Stream one turn. Yields typed SSE events, never raw text."""

    # 1. Authorize THIS conversation on THIS turn — sharing and revocation
    #    happen between turns, so a session-time check is not enough.
    await conversations.authorize(principal, req.conversation_id)

    # 2. Idempotency before any spend; a retry must not re-charge tokens.
    existing = await conversations.find_turn(req.conversation_id, req.client_message_id)
    if existing is not None:
        yield {"type": "done", "status": existing["status"], "replayed": True}
        return

    # 3. Input policy before any egress; a blocked turn creates no state.
    verdict = await policy.scan_input(principal, req.text, req.attachment_ids)
    if not verdict.allowed:
        await audit.emit(principal, "turn.blocked", req.conversation_id, "deny", verdict.reason)
        yield {"type": "blocked", "reason": verdict.reason}
        return

    turn_id = await conversations.begin_turn(principal, req)

    # 4. Assemble with the PRINCIPAL — retrieval permissions derive from the
    #    asking human, never the assistant's author or a service account.
    ctx = await assembler.build(principal, req.conversation_id, req.text, verdict.classification)

    # 5. Admit on real input size — the raw message under-counts retrieval-heavy turns.
    await quota.admit(principal, ctx.input_tokens)

    # 6. Route on classification first, cost second. A cheaper provider that is
    #    not approved for restricted data is not cheaper; it is an incident.
    route = await router.choose(classification=verdict.classification,
                                input_tokens=ctx.input_tokens)
    yield {"type": "route", "model": route["model"]}
    for citation in ctx.citations:            # provenance before tokens
        yield {"type": "citation", **citation}

    # 7. Stream with a sliding scan. One token cannot be judged; buffering the
    #    whole answer would destroy the TTFT the product lives on.
    emitted, window, status = [], "", "complete"
    try:
        async for chunk in router.stream(route, ctx):
            window += chunk
            if len(window) >= SCAN_WINDOW:
                if not policy.scan_output_window(window).allowed:
                    raise TurnBlocked("output_policy")
                window = window[-SCAN_OVERLAP:]
            emitted.append(chunk)
            yield {"type": "token", "text": chunk}
        if not policy.scan_output_window(window).allowed:
            raise TurnBlocked("output_policy")

    except TurnBlocked as blocked:
        status = "blocked"
        yield {"type": "blocked", "reason": blocked.reason, "partial": True}
    except Exception:                          # provider died mid-stream
        status = "failed"
        yield {"type": "error", "retryable": True}

    finally:
        # 8. Finalize on EVERY path — complete, blocked or failed. A turn that
        #    vanishes without a record is both a billing hole and an audit hole.
        usage = {"input": ctx.input_tokens, "output": len(emitted)}
        await conversations.finalize_turn(turn_id, status=status, text="".join(emitted),
                                          citations=ctx.citations, usage=usage, route=route)
        await quota.record(principal, usage)
        await audit.emit(principal, "turn.completed", turn_id, status)

    yield {"type": "done", "status": status}

This is a condensed sketch; a production build adds typed protocols and fuller comments.

The lines that carry the design
  • authorize(...) runs first, on every turn. A common slip is to check access when the session opens and then stop checking.
  • assembler.build(principal, …): if you remember one line, make it this one. What the turn may see is derived from the person asking.
  • quota.admit(…, ctx.input_tokens) comes after assembly, because the turns that pull in the most retrieved text are the expensive ones.
  • router.choose(classification=…): data classification wins over price when picking a model.
  • SCAN_OVERLAP: without it, a secret split across two scan windows gets through. Teams ship this bug all the time.
  • finally: every path finalises the turn, records usage and writes audit. Code without this block would not survive in production.
Idempotency, versioning, concurrency: three places, three reasons

  • Assistant publishes: if two admins edit at once, neither may quietly clobber the other's change.
  • Retention policy: years later, legal will want to know which policy was in force when a record was created.

sections.text: 8. Interview Walkthrough and Trade-OffsTwo failure modes to avoid The feature list: you tick off chat, RAG (retrieval-augmented generation), voice, images, memory and assistants, and time runs out before permissions come up. The lockdown: a tightly governed product that nobody adopts, while the risk stays in the proxy logs. Fix: say both bars aloud and keep returning to them. They hold the answer together. 50-minute plan Min Do 0–5 Set out the outcome; name the two bars and where they clash 5–12 Discovery, and bring up build-vs-buy before you are asked 12–18 Sizing: 800 concurrent streams first, then provider TPM 18–28 Architecture in dependency order; the coherence rule 28–36 Argue the five trade-offs 36–43 Failure walkthroughs; start with the over-scoped assistant 43–47 Delivery: four phases, measured gates, and config vs. adapter vs. core 47–50 Wrap up: built, left out, first production gate Five trade-offs, balanced Buy vs. build. Plenty of candidates never raise it, so bringing it up first stands out. Buying gives a mature product in weeks; the vendor runs the models and carries much of the compliance. Building gives connectors and deployments no vendor offers, and control of the data path. Recommend a hybrid: buy the model; build orchestration, connectors and governance. Building because it sounds fun is disqualifying. Vendor API vs. self-hosted. An API gives top quality for the effort and no GPUs to run, but data leaves your network and the per-token bill climbs with success. Self-hosting gives a hard boundary, flat cost at volume and an air-gap option, but a lower quality ceiling and an upgrade load teams underrate. Begin with the API behind an abstraction, and run your own models only where a data class demands it. Full history vs. compaction. Sending everything is simple and exact, but cost grows quadratically and one day the context overflows, quietly and badly. Compaction holds cost near flat and lets chats run on, though a detail sometimes drops out. Launch with the sliding window, add summarisation when telemetry asks for it, and keep the head pinned. Always-on vs. tool-invoked retrieval. Retrieving on every turn grounds answers reliably, yet "rewrite this paragraph" needs no corpus search. A model-invoked tool is cheaper and quicker, but its choice can misfire either way and it opens a path for injection. Middle route: a cheap intent classifier plus a narrow retrieval tool whose output still passes the permission filter. The number to cite: retrieval taking 400 ms consumes about 40% of a TTFT budget of 1 second. Strict DLP vs. adoption. Each false positive teaches staff the approved tool is unreliable. A handful sends them back to consumer tools, and the exposure returns in full. Tier the response: hard blocks for narrow, clear-cut categories; warn and log for vague ones; a named owner for the false-positive rate. The MVP (minimum viable product) has no write tools. Permission filtering caps the prize at what that user could already open. My eval set carries canaries. A better system prompt doesn't fix it." eDiscovery? "Each conversation carries a retention class. A legal hold beats every deletion path. A privileged endpoint needs a case reference. We audit the search and each conversation opened, because someone will ask who read an employee's chats. We rehearse it before launch. Some jurisdictions need works-council agreement first." Provider down? "Trip the breaker and move to the secondary or a smaller model. Users see a clear label instead of an error screen. Background jobs get shed. Retries are capped and jittered, and no message is lost. A game day proves it; failover that has never been exercised is just a guess." Cost runaway? "Cap tokens and concurrency for each user, give departments budgets, compact history, lay out context so the cache hits, and tier models by task. And kill the upstream stream when the client drops, or you pay for tokens no one reads." How do you know it's working? "First, egress in the proxy logs, measured before day one. Next, weekly active use, because uptake is what makes us safe. Then how often people regenerate, as a hidden quality signal. And permission-boundary violations held at zero, each one an incident." "The data model is just conversations in a Postgres table." "Messages form a tree. Retention is a named class. A hold beats deletion. Status separates complete, blocked and failed." sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.text: Key Takeaways The result owed is AI use moved off consumer tools (a ChatGPT clone is only the feature), so hold two bars at once: nothing leaves without an agreement we control, and time to first token near what the free tools give. Measure success with consumer-AI egress already in the proxy logs, aiming for an 80% cut within two quarters while weekly active use reaches 50%. Raise build vs. buy before you are asked; the honest answer is a hybrid that buys the model and builds orchestration, connectors and governance. Size on open streams, not request rate: 40 turns a second held for 20 seconds is 800 concurrent connections, and that figure sets the relay tier and the load balancer limits. At about 5.8M tokens a minute at peak, the provider's TPM quota binds first, and that limit lives in a contract, not a cluster. Resending full history makes input grow quadratically, so keep a sliding window with a pinned head and put stable content in a cacheable prefix from day one. Re-authorise the conversation on every turn, because people share and revoke access between turns. Derive retrieval permissions from the person asking: an assistant's effective scope is its scope intersected with the viewer's live permissions, so a scope caps access and never grants it. Treat index ACLs (access control lists) as a cheap pre-filter only; the check that decides runs against live permissions and drops any chunk it cannot resolve. Scan streamed output in sliding windows of 256 with an overlap of 64, so a secret split across a boundary cannot slip through and the answer still streams. A stream that opens with 200 and stops at token 300 has failed, so the SLI (service level indicator) counts done events and every path, complete, blocked or failed, finalises the turn, records usage and writes audit. If the audit write fails the turn fails too, because this platform exists to be defensible. Assume injection sometimes succeeds and make it worthless: untrusted content has no authority, the MVP has no write tools, and permission filtering caps the prize. When the provider fails, trip a breaker and move to a secondary or smaller model with a label, because an error page sends staff back to the consumer tool. Roll out in four phases that each add one class of risk, gated on measurements such as zero permission-boundary violations, and read the DLP block rate together with its false-positive rate.

sections.title: Strong discovery questions
sections.text: Strong discovery questions Where do the models come from: a commercial API, our own hosting, or a mix split by data classification? One answer means weeks of orchestration work; the other means quarters spent running a GPU fleet. Should the first release be plain chat, or grounded in company systems from day one? If grounded, which three systems go first? How long do we keep conversations? Who is allowed to read another employee's history, and through which legal process? May any employee publish an assistant, or does each one go through a review before it is published? Is corporate SSO (single sign-on) the only identity source? Do residency rules or works councils limit the usage telemetry we can collect? What stops us licensing the enterprise tier from a vendor? Everything about build versus buy turns on that. How much traffic goes to consumer AI tools today, measured? Is that number already sitting in the proxy logs? How quickly does the free tool on employees' phones show its first token? That is the speed we compete with.

sections.title: Strong functional requirements
sections.text: Strong functional requirements Core workflow: an employee asks a question; the platform grounds it only in systems that person may read and streams back a cited answer, all under policy. Set identity when the session starts, then check authorisation again on every turn. Login is not a one-time pass. Apply the caller's current permissions to retrieval at query time. A chunk the employee could not open must never be used as evidence. Allow departments to publish assistants. What an assistant can reach in practice is its own scope intersected with the permissions of whoever is using it. Classify each input before it is dispatched and scan the output as it streams. When something is blocked or redacted, record that decision. Write each turn to an audit log that can only be appended to. When an administrator reads an employee's conversation, that read is logged too.

sections.title: Strong non-functional requirements
sections.text: Strong non-functional requirements Latency: time-to-first-token is the SLO (service level objective) that drives adoption. I'd hold p95 below 1.0s and keep p99 below 2.0s. Past about a second, people start to feel the wait. Next to the free tool, a four-second spinner would look broken. Availability: the case puts daily volume near 576,000 turns. Squeeze them into a ten-hour working day and you get 40 turns per second; the morning rush runs at 2.5x, with roughly 800 streams open at once. Security: each isolation layer fails closed. Here, failing open means leaking. Compliance: retention is a named policy class that supports legal hold. The audit must cover 100% of the turns we serve. Reliability: the message a user typed must never be lost. When the main model is in trouble, fall back to a smaller model and label it, instead of showing an error page. Cost: if every turn resends the whole history, each turn's input grows linearly and the conversation's total grows quadratically. So keep the head pinned, summarise the middle, and design a stable, cacheable prefix from the start.

sections.title: Architecture explanation
sections.text: Architecture explanation Before drawing any boxes, state the coherence rule. Identity is set at the session and checked again on each turn. Nothing reaches the context window unless it has passed policy and been audited. At the edge, a gateway validates each SSO token and shapes the traffic. Conversation state belongs to the conversation service, which authorises the caller on every turn. At the centre of the design sits the context assembler, where permissions, cost, safety and quality all meet. It builds context from the identity of the human asking, and ignores whatever the client claims. Retrieval and the connectors fetch candidates already filtered by the caller's current permissions. If the ACL (access control list) resolver is down, the chunk is dropped; access never widens. Inputs pass through policy and DLP (data loss prevention) classification before anything is dispatched. The same layer scans the streamed output through a sliding window whose overlap is at least as long as the longest pattern, so a known pattern split across a boundary still gets caught. The model router picks the provider, deployment and model from the data class, cost and health, and data class always beats cost. Provider adapters hide vendor differences and take care of retries. The streaming relay keeps long-lived connections open and deals with aborts mid-stream. When a client disconnects, it cancels the upstream stream, so we stop paying for tokens nobody will read, at least on providers that honour cancellation. Some do not. The assistant registry controls definitions and scopes. Usage and quota metering counts tokens. An append-only audit pipeline records each turn, admin reads included.

sections.title: Data model / integration assumptions
sections.text: Data model / integration assumptions Conversation(id, workspace_id, owner_id, assistant_id, retention_class, legal_hold); Message(id, conversation_id, parent_id, role, content_ref, citations, token_count, model_id, status); Assistant(id, author_id, instructions, tool_bindings, data_scopes, visibility, version, review_state); Attachment(id, uploader_id, scan_status, extract_ref); AuditEvent(event_id, actor_id, action, resource_ref, decision, reason). Messages form a tree rather than a list. parent_id lets a user regenerate an answer or branch the conversation. status has four values: complete, blocked, failed and partial. A stream that dies at 80% fits none of the first three. retention_class holds a named policy, not a raw number. Years later, legal can still say which policy applied. scan_status decides whether an attachment may enter the context window. If the scan fails, we treat the file as untrusted, not merely as missing.

sections.title: Red-team risks
sections.text: Red-team risks assistants with too much scope laundering access, ACLs left stale after a revocation, prompt injection through documents, the head of the prompt truncated without notice, scripted accounts running away with usage The permission laundromat: an employee with wide access publishes an assistant to the whole company. So intersect its data scope with each viewer's own permissions. A revocation happens, but a cached permission lives on. The employee then sees a document they can no longer open, through a stale ACL. A document someone uploads, or one retrieval pulls in, contains an indirect prompt injection. It must have no authority over policy or tool calls. On a long conversation, a naive drop-from-front strategy cuts off the system prompt. The assistant's behaviour changes and nobody can see why. The audit pipeline fails. The turn must fail with it rather than go ahead unrecorded, because the design allows no backfill.

sections.title: Rollout plan
sections.text: Rollout plan Week 0-1: take a baseline of consumer-AI egress from the proxy logs. Agree governance and adoption as one shared target with two bars. Week 1-2: release plain chat first. SSO, quotas, retention classes and audit are all live before grounding exists. Week 2-3: ground answers in the first corpus. A contract test over titles and snippets shows that permissions are filtered at query time. Week 3-4: keep the gate shut until there are no permission-boundary violations and citation click-through shows people trust the grounding. Week 5: open up file attachments. Each one is scanned for malware and has its text extracted, and only a passing scan status lets it into the context. Week 6-8: let reviewed assistants be published, and check scope intersection with the viewer on each turn. After pilot: add more corpora only as long as egress keeps falling, weekly active use keeps rising and audit completeness holds at 100%.

sections.title: Final 2-minute spoken answer
sections.text: Final 2-minute spoken answerI wouldn't open with the model. On paper, 40,000 employees want "build us our own ChatGPT". The real driver, though, is the egress report: 6,400 staff already paste company data into consumer AI tools. So the business goal is to bring that usage onto a platform we govern, without losing what made the consumer tools appealing. That sets two bars, and they pull against each other. Data leaves our boundary only under an agreement we control. The first token has to arrive about as fast as it does on the free app in their pocket. It also hands us a rare thing, a success metric whose baseline we already measure. My proposed target: within two quarters, measured consumer-AI egress falls by 80% and weekly active use reaches 50%. Locking everything down won't get us there, and neither will shipping without governance. For the architecture, I'd state the coherence rule before any diagram. Identity is set at the session and checked again on each turn. Nothing enters the context window unless it has passed policy and been written to the audit. The context assembler sits at the centre, where permissions, cost, safety and quality meet. Permissions always come from the human asking. A published assistant can therefore reach only the overlap of its own scope and the viewer's, and that stops one privileged person laundering their access to everyone. Retrieval resolves ACLs at query time. If the resolver is down, the chunk is dropped. Every layer fails closed, because here failing open means leaking. The order of release is general chat, grounding, attachments and finally assistants, so each phase brings in only one new class of risk.
